summary: Specifies how a server should behave to serve WebNFS clients. It is the server-side companion to the WebNFS client specification and is informational.

eli5.summary: This is the instruction sheet for the server that hands out files to WebNFS-using computers.

questions: how does a webnfs server work
subtitle: How servers support web browsers accessing NFS filesystems

tldr.problem: Standard NFS clients need to use the MOUNT protocol to get started and contact a portmap service to find the NFS port, which is slow and doesn't work well through firewalls or for web browsers.
tldr.mechanism: WebNFS servers support a public filehandle and multi-component path lookup, letting clients start directly on well-known port 2049 without portmap or MOUNT, and traverse entire paths in one request.
tldr.outcome: Web browsers and simple clients can access NFS filesystems faster with better firewall compatibility and lower server overhead.

today: RFC 2055 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. WebNFS remains part of NFS protocol suites, though in practice many web-based file sharing scenarios now use HTTP-based protocols like WebDAV or REST APIs rather than WebNFS.

sections.title: What WebNFS Servers Do
sections.content:
WebNFS extends NFS versions 2 and 3 with features that make them easier to use from web browsers and simple clients. A WebNFS server implements semantic extensions so that clients can skip the usual setup protocols (MOUNT and portmap) and start requesting files directly.

This specification describes what a WebNFS server must do. It is the counterpart to RFC 2054, which describes WebNFS clients. Implementing these features lets servers be faster, more scalable, and easier for clients to reach through firewalls.
sections.eli5: WebNFS is a simpler way to use NFS that works better for web browsers and lets you skip steps that usually slow things down.

sections.title: The Public Filehandle and Port
sections.content:
In standard NFS, a client must first use the MOUNT protocol to get a filehandle for an exported directory. WebNFS clients skip this by using a public filehandle, a special reserved filehandle value that the server always accepts. For NFS version 2, the public filehandle is 32 zero bytes. For version 3, it is a zero-length filehandle.

WebNFS servers listen on the well-known port 2049 for both TCP and UDP, eliminating the need to query the portmap service. Servers should support both TCP (preferred for wide-area networks with reliability and congestion control) and UDP (for backward compatibility), but clients try TCP first.
sections.eli5: The public filehandle is a magic starting point that tells the server "I do not have permission yet, let me in anyway." The server is always listening on port 2049, so clients do not have to hunt for it.

sections.title: Multi-component Lookup
sections.content:
Normally, NFS LOOKUP requests handle one pathname component at a time. To find a file at "a/b/c", a client must send three separate LOOKUP requests: one for "a", one for "b", and one for "c", each using the filehandle returned by the previous request.

WebNFS servers support multi-component lookup on the public filehandle: a client can send a LOOKUP request with multiple components like "a/b/c" and the server returns the filehandle of the final component in a single request. This reduces latency and network traffic significantly.
sections.eli5: Instead of asking the server three times to find your way through folders a, then b, then c, you can ask all at once: "where is a/b/c?"

sections.title: Canonical and Native Path Syntax
sections.content:
WebNFS supports two path syntaxes. A canonical path is slash-separated (like "dir/file") and is URL-encoded to handle non-ASCII and special characters: the forward slash is encoded as %2f, non-printable ASCII characters (0x00-0x1f and 0x7f) are encoded with %, and the % character itself is %25. Canonical paths starting with / are relative to the server's root; others are relative to the public filehandle's directory.

A native path is the server's own pathname syntax (e.g., "dir:file" on some systems). It is indicated by starting the pathname with the byte 0x80 followed by the native-syntax path. The server can return an error for unknown path formats (bytes 0x81-0xff).
sections.eli5: WebNFS supports the usual folder/file path style, and also lets you give the server a path in its own language, like if the server uses colons instead of slashes.

sections.title: Symbolic Links and Export Boundaries
sections.content:
When evaluating a multi-component path, the server must follow symbolic links as part of the pathname evaluation, rather than asking the client to do it. However, if the final component is a symbolic link, the server returns its filehandle and lets the client decide what to do.

A server may encounter paths that reference files outside the exported hierarchy. If the destination is not exported, the server must return an error. Servers that check client access on every NFS request (not just at MOUNT time) can safely return filehandles for paths spanning multiple exports. Servers that rely on MOUNT for access checking cannot, because WebNFS clients do not use MOUNT.
sections.eli5: The server can follow shortcuts (symbolic links) inside a path, but if you ask for a file that is not supposed to be shared, the server says no. The rules are stricter for servers that do not use the MOUNT protocol for permission checks.

sections.title: Additional Features and Considerations
sections.content:
A WebNFS server can associate the public filehandle with any exported directory. For example, an administrator can attach it to an FTP archive root so that FTP-style paths access NFS files. Servers that support spanning paths can attach the public filehandle to the filesystem root, and clients can navigate to any exported directory beneath it.

WebNFS servers may optionally emulate HTTP index files: when a multi-component lookup finds a directory, the server can check for an index file (like index.html) and return its filehandle instead of the directory. The server must not check the originating port number of requests, since WebNFS clients are not required to use privileged ports. Security considerations for NFS versions 2 and 3 apply, including provisions for optional negotiation of secure connection schemes.
sections.eli5: The admin can put the public filehandle anywhere on the server. The server can act a bit like a web server by automatically serving index files. And the server does not require clients to use special ports.
